code.title: Copy constructor vs copy assignment: which one runs

followUps: Because passing by value would need the copy constructor to copy its own argument, which calls the copy constructor again, forever. Taking const T& breaks that loop: no copy is made to receive the source, and const lets it bind to temporaries and const objects too. The compiler even rejects T(T) as a copy constructor. Example: T b = a; binds a reference to a, then copies its fields once.

So that assignments can be chained and used in expressions, and so it behaves like built-in types. Returning *this by reference lets a = b = c; work: it parses as a = (b = c), and the inner call must hand back something assignable. With void, that chain would not compile. Returning by value would make an extra copy; returning a reference costs nothing.

T& operator=(const T& o) { /* copy */ return *this; }

No. Since C++17, T b = T(); is guaranteed copy elision: the temporary is not a separate object, and b is constructed directly from the initializer, so only the default constructor runs. The copy or move constructor does not even need to be accessible. Before C++17 the copy was permitted to be elided but still had to exist. The same applies to returning a prvalue such as return T();.

code.title: Shallow copy aliases, deep copy owns

followUps: Do it in two passes with a map from old node to new node. Pass 1: walk the list, create a copy of every node, and store map[old] = copy. Pass 2: walk again and set copy->next = map[old->next] and copy->random = map[old->random]. For 5 nodes that is 5 allocations and 10 lookups. Cost: O(N) time and O(N) extra space for the map; an interleaving trick (insert each copy after its original) cuts the extra space to O(1).

Because copy-on-write breaks guarantees that C++11 added: iterators, references and pointers into a string must stay valid until a modifying call, and operator[] on a non-const string must not invalidate others. With a shared buffer, even s[0] might have to unshare and reallocate, invalidating the other copies' references, and the reference count must be atomic for threads. So libstdc++ moved to small-string optimization and a new ABI.

Give the base class a virtual clone() that each derived class implements by copying itself, because only the derived class knows its own type. Then base->clone() returns a new object of the right dynamic type. Copying with Base b2 = *p; would slice instead. Example: if p points to a Circle of radius 3, p->clone() yields a new Circle of radius 3. It costs one heap allocation and one virtual call per copy.

virtual std::unique_ptr<Base> clone() const = 0;

code.title: Rule of Five and Rule of Zero in practice

followUps: Declaring a copy constructor, copy assignment, move assignment or destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor. Declaring a move constructor or move assignment also deletes the implicit copy operations. So a class with only a user-written destructor, such as ~T() { log(); }, silently loses its moves, and std::move(t) then falls back to copying. Every member is copied, e.g. a vector of 1000 ints is copied rather than having its pointer stolen. Fix it by writing T(T&&) = default;.

Yes, ~T() = default; written in the class counts as user-declared, so it suppresses the implicit move operations just like a hand-written destructor. The move constructor is then not generated and std::move copies instead. This is a common trap when you add a virtual destructor to a base class: virtual ~Base() = default; removes its moves, so you must re-add Base(Base&&) = default; and the copy operations too.

A move-only wrapper owns the resource, deletes the copies, and transfers ownership in the move operations. After a move the source must hold nothing, so its destructor does nothing.

class Handle {
  int* p;
public:
  explicit Handle(int v) : p(new int(v)) {}
  Handle(const Handle&) = delete;
  Handle& operator=(const Handle&) = delete;
  Handle(Handle&& o) noexcept : p(std::exchange(o.p, nullptr)) {}
  Handle& operator=(Handle&& o) noexcept { std::swap(p, o.p); return *this; }
  ~Handle() { delete p; }
};

code.title: std::move is only a cast

followUps: Because it blocks copy elision and can force a worse operation. For return local; the compiler can construct the local directly in the caller's slot (NRVO), or at least treats it as an rvalue automatically. Writing std::move(local) changes the expression type to T&&, which is no longer the plain local name, so NRVO is disabled and a move constructor is called. Moving is cheap, but zero work beats it. Compilers warn with -Wpessimizing-move.

It silently copies instead of moving. std::move(c) on a const T gives const T&&, which cannot bind to T(T&&) because that would drop const. It can bind to T(const T&), so the copy constructor runs, with no error or warning. For a const std::string of 1000 characters you pay a full 1000-character copy. Avoid moving const objects; the clue is a move that does not empty the source.

std::forward<T>(x) passes an argument on with the same value category it came in with: lvalue stays lvalue, rvalue stays rvalue. It is used in templates with forwarding references T&&, because inside the function the name x is always an lvalue. std::move always casts to rvalue, std::forward only does so when the caller passed an rvalue. It is how make_unique and emplace_back hand arguments to constructors without extra copies.

template<class T> void wrap(T&& x) { f(std::forward<T>(x)); }

code.title: noexcept move decides vector reallocation

followUps: The program calls std::terminate, which by default aborts the process. A noexcept function promises not to let an exception escape; if one does, the stack is not guaranteed to unwind and there is no catch. The compiler checks nothing at compile time, so it is a runtime promise. Example: a noexcept move constructor whose new throws bad_alloc kills the program. This is why moves should only be marked noexcept when they truly cannot fail.

No. std::list and std::deque never relocate existing elements when they grow, because each element lives in its own node or block. Appending to a list of 1000 items moves nothing, so a throwing move does not threaten the strong guarantee. Only contiguous reallocating containers, mainly std::vector (and std::string-like buffers), use move_if_noexcept when growing. Moves still matter for list when you insert by moving a value in.

Write noexcept after the declaration: T(T&&) noexcept = default;. A defaulted move is already noexcept when all bases and members have noexcept moves, so you normally just default it and check with static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>). The explicit form states your intent in the declaration and documents it for readers; check it with the static_assert.

code.title: A hand-built vtable and the cost of a vptr

followUps: Two vptrs, usually: one per polymorphic base subobject, because each base needs a vtable laid out as that base expects. With struct C : A, B where both have virtuals, the A subobject sits at offset 0 and shares C's primary vptr, while the B subobject has its own vptr. On 64-bit that is 16 bytes of vptrs. Converting C* to B* adds an offset to the pointer so B's vptr is found.

A thunk is a tiny compiler-generated stub that adjusts the this pointer, then jumps to the real function. It is needed when a base subobject is not at offset 0: calling a virtual through a B* hands the function a pointer to the B part, but the override is written for the whole C. The thunk subtracts the offset, for example 8 bytes, and jumps to C::f. Covariant return types may also need thunks.

Because during construction the object only has the parts built so far, and virtual calls must not reach members that do not exist yet. Each constructor in the chain sets the vptr to its own class's vtable at the start. In Base() the vptr points to Base's table; then Derived() runs and resets it to Derived's table. Destruction does the reverse. So a virtual call inside Base() calls Base::f, never the derived override.

code.title: Override, overload and hiding

followUps:
Yes, but the derived overloads hide the base ones, so you must bring them back with a using-declaration. Writing using Base::f; inside the derived class makes all base overloads visible next to the new one. Example: Base has virtual f(int) and f(double); Derived overrides only f(int). Without the using line, d.f(1.5) would convert to int and call Derived::f(int). With it, f(double) is found.

struct D : Base { void f(int) override; using Base::f; };

Use -Woverloaded-virtual on GCC (included in -Wall from GCC 13) and Clang's -Woverloaded-virtual, which warn when a derived function hides a base virtual. -Wsuggest-override (GCC) and -Winconsistent-missing-override (Clang) flag a missing override, which is the best defence because the compiler then errors on any signature mismatch. MSVC gives warning C4263 or C4264 for hidden virtuals. Treat these warnings as errors in CI.

No, default arguments are static: they are chosen at compile time from the static type of the expression, while the function body is chosen at runtime from the dynamic type. If Base declares virtual void f(int x = 1) and Derived overrides it with f(int x = 2), then Base* p = new Derived; p->f(); runs Derived::f with x equal to 1. Avoid different defaults in overrides; use overloads or non-virtual wrappers.

code.title: Abstract class with a pure virtual body

followUps: Use a class with only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor, with no data members. Derived classes implement everything, and callers use pointers or references to it. Example: struct Logger { virtual void log(const std::string&) = 0; virtual ~Logger() = default; };. Make the destructor public and virtual if users may delete through it, or protected and non-virtual otherwise. Mark copy operations deleted to avoid slicing.

NVI (non-virtual interface) means the public function is non-virtual and calls a private virtual hook that derived classes override. The base class keeps control of the fixed steps around the customisation point, such as locking, logging or checking conditions. Example: void save() { validate(); doSave(); log(); } with virtual void doSave() = 0; private. It gives one place to add pre- and post-conditions and keeps the public interface stable.

Use an abstract class for runtime polymorphism: the concrete type is chosen while running, objects live in a mixed container, or the code is in a compiled library boundary. Use a concept for compile-time polymorphism: templates need a certain set of operations, no inheritance is needed, and calls can be inlined with no vptr. A concept cannot make a std::vector of mixed types. Cost: abstract class means a virtual call, concept means code duplicated per type.

code.title: Virtual destructor and deleting via base

followUps: Yes, a shared pointer made from shared_ptr<Base>(new Derived) is safe. The shared_ptr constructor is a template that remembers the real type Derived in its control block deleter, so it deletes through Derived* and the right destructor runs. The same holds for make_shared<Derived>(). It would leak only if you first converted to a raw Base* and built the shared_ptr<Base> from that. unique_ptr<Base> has no such memory and needs the virtual destructor.

It is the compiler-generated function that is called by delete on a polymorphic object. It is a virtual destructor variant that first runs the complete destructor, then calls operator delete with the right address and size. The Itanium ABI emits three destructor entries: the complete-object destructor, the base-object destructor, and the deleting destructor, which sits in the vtable slot. This is how delete basePtr frees the whole derived object, not just the base part.

You should not, because std::vector has a non-virtual destructor and is not designed as a base class. Deleting a derived object through vector* is undefined behaviour, and nothing stops callers from slicing. Use composition: hold a vector as a member and expose only the functions you want. If you only want extra algorithms, write free functions. Private inheritance or a wrapper class are fine when you need to adjust the interface.

code.title: Constructor and destructor order, virtual calls inside

followUps: The compiler warns that members are initialised in a different order than the initializer list says. Members are always constructed in declaration order, not in the order you wrote the list. If int a; int b; are declared that way and the constructor says : b(1), a(b + 1), then a is set first from an uninitialised b, which is a bug. The fix is to list initializers in declaration order. Enable with -Wall, which includes -Wreorder.

Because Java runs the overridden method of the most derived class even while the derived fields are not yet set, so it can see null or zero fields. In C++ the object's dynamic type is the class being constructed, so the virtual call stays in the base and never touches uninitialised derived members. It is safer but surprising: in C++ the call in Base() does Base::f, even when Derived overrides it. If the base version is pure virtual, the program aborts with a pure virtual call error.

Two-phase initialization means the constructor only sets up a safe basic state, and a separate function such as init() does the work that needs virtual dispatch or can fail. The caller or a factory runs both steps. Example: static std::unique_ptr<Base> create() { auto p = std::make_unique<D>(); p->init(); return p; }. Now init() can call virtual functions safely because the object is fully built. The cost is that objects may exist in a half-ready state, so hide the constructor and use the factory.

code.title: Object slicing and its fixes

followUps: Because after slicing the object really is a Base: the derived part does not exist any more. static_cast<Derived&>(sliced) compiles, but it is undefined behaviour, since it reads memory that was never part of the object. Example: a Dog with a 32-byte name copied into an Animal of 8 bytes keeps only the 8-byte base; the cast would read 24 bytes beyond it. The data is lost for good, so the only fix is to avoid slicing by using references or pointers.

Catching by value slices the exception object, and a bare throw; rethrows the original exception object, not your sliced copy. So if you catch (Base e) a Derived and then write throw;, the outer handler still gets the full Derived. But if you write throw e;, it throws a new Base copy and the derived part is lost. Always catch by const reference and use plain throw;.

catch (const Base& e) { log(e); throw; }

std::polymorphic<T> (C++26) is a value-like owner of a T or any class derived from it. Copying it deep-copies the pointed-to object using the dynamic type, so you can write std::vector<std::polymorphic<Shape>> with value semantics and no slicing. It stores the object on the heap and records a copier internally, replacing hand-written clone() functions. It is like unique_ptr that copies, and a moved-from one is valueless.

code.title: Canonical operator overloads

followUps: Hidden friends are friend functions defined inside the class body that are found only through argument-dependent lookup. They are preferred because they do not pollute the enclosing namespace, give fewer overload candidates, and compile faster. They still allow conversions on both operands, since they are non-members. Example: friend bool operator==(const P& a, const P& b) { return a.x == b.x; } is found for P arguments only.

Do not overload &&, || and the comma operator, because the overloaded versions lose short-circuit evaluation and guaranteed order of evaluation, so a && b would evaluate both sides. Also avoid unary & (address-of), since it breaks generic code that takes addresses. You also cannot overload ::, ., .*, ?: and sizeof. Overload operators only when the meaning is the obvious one.

Because a non-explicit operator bool allows silent conversions to int and so enables nonsense like obj + 1, obj1 == obj2 comparing two booleans, or passing the object where an integer is expected. With explicit operator bool() const the conversion still works in conditions such as if (p), while (p) and !p, but not in arithmetic or in assignment to an int. That is how std::unique_ptr and streams do it.

code.title: Defaulted and hand-written operator<=>

followUps: The comparator must be a strict weak ordering: irreflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, and with transitive equivalence. If not, the behaviour of std::sort, std::map and std::set is undefined: it can loop forever, crash by reading past the array end, or silently give wrong order. The classic bug is using <= as the comparator: comp(a, a) is true, which violates irreflexivity, and sorting with many equal values can crash.

Because equality and ordering can have different costs and meanings, so a user-written <=> may not imply a correct ==. Generating a == b from (a <=> b) == 0 would be slow for strings, where lengths can be compared first. Only a defaulted <=> also declares a defaulted ==. If you write your own <=>, add bool operator==(const T&) const yourself, or == will not compile.

A defaulted <=> on a struct with a double member returns std::partial_ordering, because NaN is unordered with everything. Comparing NaN <=> 1.0 gives unordered, and then <, >, <= and >= are all false. The defaulted == is also false for two NaNs, so x == x fails. Never put such a type in a sorted container unless you exclude NaN; use std::strong_order or std::total_order for a full order on doubles.

code.title: Exception-safe copy assignment

followUps: Basic: no leaks and no broken invariants after an exception, but the state may have changed. Strong: the operation either succeeds or leaves the object exactly as it was (commit or rollback). Nothrow: the operation never throws, as with swap or destructors. Example: when vec = other throws bad_alloc half way, a strong guarantee keeps the old contents, while basic only promises a valid vector with unknown contents. Write the risky part first, then commit with non-throwing steps.

Because if (this != &o) only protects against self-assignment, not against exceptions. In code such as delete[] d; d = new int[o.n]; the old buffer is freed first, so if new throws, d is a dangling pointer and the object is broken. The right order is: allocate and copy into a temporary, then release the old one, then adopt the new one. With that order the self-check becomes just an optimisation.

It reuses its existing capacity when it can, so it avoids reallocating. If the source has more elements than the capacity, it allocates new storage, copies, and frees the old; otherwise it copy-assigns the overlapping part and constructs or destroys the rest. That is faster than copy-and-swap but gives only the basic guarantee, because elements may be half assigned when an element copy throws. Self-assignment is safe and does nothing.

code.title: Cloning a polymorphic object

followUps: A covariant return type has to be a pointer or reference to a class derived from the base's return type, and unique_ptr<Derived> is a different class type from unique_ptr<Base>, not a derived class of it. They merely convert. So a Derived::clone() returning unique_ptr<Derived> does not override a base virtual returning unique_ptr<Base>. The usual fix is a private virtual clone_impl() returning a raw pointer, wrapped by a public non-virtual clone().

Small-buffer optimisation stores small objects inside the handle itself instead of allocating on the heap. The type-erased wrapper has, say, 32 bytes of aligned storage; if sizeof(T) fits and the move is noexcept, it constructs T there with placement new, else it uses new. This saves an allocation per object, which is why std::function and std::any are often fast for small lambdas. The cost is a larger handle and extra code for the two paths.

Give every class a virtual serialize() that writes a type tag first, then its fields, and keep a registry (a factory map) from tag to a function that builds the right object when reading. Example: Circle writes "circle", 3; the reader looks up "circle" and calls its factory. The tag must stay stable across versions. Libraries like protobuf or std::variant with an index achieve the same with less code.
